The Graduate Certificate in Community Planning (CP) is an online program that helps students develop core competencies in sustainable Community Planning.
Through this program, students will gain a foundation in the principles and practices of community planning and development, specifically in areas of land use and environmental planning.
The history of planning has many examples of environmental injustice, in which land use decisions have privileged some communities over others.
A commitment to anti-racism, inclusiveness, equity, as well as spatial and social justice perspectives is an integral part of a planning education.
Students can earn their certificate in four sessions, maximizing flexibility and convenience for career enhancement, leadership positions in the industry, and professional growth.
The Community Planning online certificate aligns with the University's commitment to urban initiative, community engagement and solving the world's most important challenges by equiping students with practical knowledge and understanding of how to plan for and enable equitable and sustainable communities.

This 4-course asychonous online graduate certificate also creates a learning opportunity for students who may not be able to attend graduate school in person on a full time basis, thereby creating a diverse learning opportunity (goal 3 of the URI Stragic Priority 2) and increase graduate student enrollment (goal 2 of Strategic Priority 2).
The impact of a working public better informed in values and strategies of community planning should contribute to healthier and more sustainable communities environmentally, socially and economically.
The online graduate Community Planning certificate will open doors for recent college graduates as well as working professionals; they will become eligible for positions and promotion in a growing job market.
By combining this online certificate with other stackable certificates such as Public Administration, MEM and GIS, students will be well equipped to engage in the significant planning challenges of our time.
Our department currently offers an in-person Graduate Certificate in Community Planning.
This proposed new program will be offered in the 7-week online format and require 4 classes with 3 required classes and one elective (12 credits).

Our existing Community Planning Graduate Certificate requires 5 courses to complete the certificate (15 or 16 credits).
The asychonous online certitificate is intended for a different student population from our in-person gradute certificate and provides somewhat different content.
The online certificate content is pragmatically planned to be useful for working professionals, adapted for online delivery, and geared towards working professionals who do not have prior knowledge of planning.
The purpose of the Certificate is to give these students a way to quickly and remotely attain a basic knowledge of planning, and to stack that knowledge with other certificates, such as Public Policy, Marine Affairs, GIS, etc.
By contrast, the full semester, in-person planning program encompasses a wide and in-depth disciplinary space, with opportunities to learn from in-person university relationships and pursue independent research, while still providing future planners with knowledge and tools for professional work.

Goal 1: Graduates will be prepared to enter research-focused graduate programs based on their knowledge of empirically- supported psychological processes and how to apply this knowledge to promote health and welfare.

Goal 3: Graduates will be able to work ethically in settings that emphasize diversity and global thinking.
The BS in Psychology is described to students as a program that focuses on the empirical and methodological aspects of psychology, that emphasizes math, science, and research methods in creating and applying psychological knowledge, and that includes a requirement in hands on research experience.
This program addresses Strategy 1 of the Agenda for Change (Infuse Anti-Racism, Social Justice and DEI Perspectives) in the Curriculum in several ways.

Mark Robbins A BS in psychology prepares students for a wide variety of career options.
According to the website of the American Psychological Association ( https://www.apa.org/ed/precollege/psn/2018/01/bachelors-degree ), about 25 percent of psychology baccalaureates go to graduate school in psychology, about 18 percent go on for more education but not in psychology, and 57 percent are workforce graduates (Lin, Christidis & Stamm, 2017).
The BS degree prepares graduates especially well to apply to doctoral or other research-oriented advanced degrees in Psychology or other fields.

For those who do not wish to obtain an advanced degree, there are many job opportunities.
The above referenced website lists 70 job titles that students with a BS in Psychology are prepared for.
The BS degree with its focus on methodology, scientific writing, and statistical analysis especially trains graduates for any type of position requiring analytic, scientific writing, or data analytic skills, such as data base design analyst, research assistant, systems analyst, technical writer, information specialist, or data base manager.
A number of these occupations are considered high impact jobs in RI.
The Occupational Outlook Handbook of the Bureau of Labor ( https://www.bls.gov/ooh/field-of- degree/psychology/psychology-field-of-degree.htm ) indicates that the median salary for those with a degree in Psychology is $50,000 and that 60% are employed in occupations requiring at least a bachelor's degree.
Many department faculty offer students the opportunity to serve as undergraduate teaching assistants for course credit.
There are no paid undergraduate assistantships.
Graduate teaching assistantships are offered to assist instructors with PSY 200, PSY 301, and PSY 435.

Among peer institutions (UMass, UConn, UVM, UNH, U of Maine, and U of Delaware) BS degrees in Psychology are offered by three (UMASS, UCONN, and UVM).
The University of Delaware offers a BS in Neuroscience but not Psychology.
UNH and U of Maine offer only BA programs.
It does not make URI unique in our region to offer this degree, but if we did not offer it, we would not be keeping up with the more research/science oriented institutions in our region.
There is a trend among peer institutions to emphasize the scientific basis of psychology, which the proposed changes to the program are designed to accomplish.

V. 24.01.26 RATIONALE There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed name change. 1.
Explain why the change of department name is being proposed.
The proposed new name of "Chemical, Biomolecular, and Materials Engineering" accurately reflects the career and technological fields that graduates enter and the research and scholarly expertise of the department faculty.
For example, the department has many graduates working at Amgen, which is a biotechnology company producing biological molecules (i.e., biomolecules), as well as Toray Plastics America, which produces polymeric materials.
The new name also reflects topics that are taught in our courses and the newly formed department Minor in Materials Engineering.
An additional Minor in Biochemical Engineering has been proposed (expected launch in Spring 2025) and a minor in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing and Formulation (includes biomolecular topics) is offered by the Department of Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences for c hemical engineering majors.

The proposed new name aligns with similar department names of URI's peer and aspiring institutions, which include terms such as "bioengineering", "biomedical", and "biological engineering" in their names preceded by the term "chemical".
Changing the department name at URI is expected to make us more competitive in undergraduate student recruiting and, coupled with the new name reflecting our research expertise, more competitive at recruiting graduate s tudents and faculty.
INSTITUTIONAL ROLE The department name change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution. 1.
Explain how the name change is consistent with published role and mission of the institution, and how it is related to institutional planning.
As with our current name, the new name will continue to align with the role and mission of the institution in providing high-quality education and solving the world's most challenging problems (the new name explicitly extends this to biomolecules and materials).

It also aligns with institutional planning, providing new opportunities to increase student recruiting, to create new degree and/or certificate programs, and to pursue interdisciplinary collaboration (funding agencies/proposal review panels link department names to expertise). 2.
Explain how the organizational change impacts other units and programs within the institution.
Have you communicated with the other units and programs and have any concerns been raised relative to the organizational change?
Describe the concerns.
The proposed name change was formally presented to the department chairs in the College of Engineering and no concerns were raised - they were collectively enthusiastic.
The potential for the most overlap is with the Biomedical Engineering program in the Department of Electrical, Computer, and Biomedical Engineering.
The CHE chair discussed the name change with the program lead for Biomedical Engineering and the only concern was with the abbreviation, CHE changing to CBME. "BME" is the abbreviation for Biomedical Engineering and the BME lead thought this could lead to confusion during registration.

After explaining that the course codes would remain "CHE" there was no longer a concern.

CONTRACTS: URI Catalog Information Honors Contracts Honors contracts allow students to earn Honors credit for non-Honors courses by pursuing more advanced study. This requires an agreement between the student and instructor, and approval from the Honors Program. This option is valuable for students interested in a course not offered in an Honors format or whose schedules prevent them from enrolling in an Honors section. The following restrictions apply. (Any exceptions must be approved in advance by the Honors Program): 1. Honors contract credits shall not amount to more than one-third (1/3) of a student’s total coursework required for graduation from Honors. 2. Students shall not engage in more than one honors contract per semester. 3. Honors contracts cannot be completed during the summer or J-Term. Nor can they be applied to 100-level courses, internships, independent studies, study abroad, or courses at other institutions. 4. Contracted courses must be taken for a letter grade and must be completed with a grade of B or better to count towards Honors Program requirements. 5. Students who do not complete the proposed work to the satisfaction of the instructor will not earn Honors credit for the course.

CONTRACTS: For the Honors Program Web site. The Honors Contract Process The Honors contract process involves four stages: 1. Crafting of an individualized project with the course instructor. 2. Submission of the contract to the Honors Program for approval. 3. Completion of the agreed-upon assignments and activities. 4. Submission of the completed work and the Honors Contract completion form conﬁrming the instructor’s satisfaction with the work. 1: Crafting the Honors Contract The Honors Contract is a mutual commitment to a learning experience above and beyond normal course requirements. The student and instructor must agree on the criteria for evaluating the project and its scheduling. Instructors are under no obligation to supervise Honors Contracts. The Honors contract is intended to enrich the student's education by further work of mutual interest to the student and instructor, rather than simply adding to the course’s workload. Students would therefore be wise to consider projects where the enriched assignment or activity also suits the interests and needs of the instructor. An Honors contract should involve 6 to 7 hours per credit: A 3-credit course should, for example, involve approximately 20 hours of additional work. These estimated hours should include 2-3 hours of meetings with the instructor: one at the start, one mid-project, and one to conclude. Overall, plan for 3-5 hours of direct faculty involvement, including evaluation.
